title: The Panthera story and the virgin birth
source_text: Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἐπανέλθωμεν εἰς τὴν τοῦ Ἰουδαίου προσωποποιΐαν, ἐν ᾗ ἀναγέγραπται ἡ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μήτηρ ὡς ἐξωσθεῖσα ὑπὸ τοῦ μνηστευσαμένου αὐτὴν τέκτονος, ἐλεγχθεῖσα ἐπὶ μοιχείᾳ καὶ τίκτουσα ἀπό τινος στρατιώτου Πανθήρα τοὔνομα· καὶ ἴδωμεν εἰ μὴ τυφλῶς οἱ μυθοποιήσαντες τὴν μοιχείαν τῆς παρθένου καὶ τοῦ Πανθήρα καὶ τὸν τέκτονα ἐξωσάμενον αὐτὴν ταῦτα πάντα ἀνέπλασαν ἐπὶ καθαιρέσει τῆς παραδόξου ἀπὸ ἁγίου πνεύματος συλλήψεως· ἐδύναντο γὰρ ἄλλως ψευδοποιῆσαι διὰ τὸ σφόδρα παράδοξον τὴν ἱστορίαν καὶ μὴ ὡσπερεὶ ἀκουσίως συγκαταθέσθαι ὅτι οὐκ ἀπὸ συνήθων ἀνθρώποις γάμων ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐγεννήθη. καὶ ἀκόλουθόν γε ἦν τοὺς μὴ συγκαταθεμένους τῇ παραδόξῳ γενέσει τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πλάσαι τι ψεῦδος· τὸ δὲ μὴ πιθανῶς αὐτοὺς τοῦτο ποιῆσαι ἀλλὰ μετὰ τοῦ τηρῆσαι ὅτι οὐκ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ παρθένος συνέλαβε τὸν Ἰησοῦν, τοῖς ἀκούειν καὶ ἐλέγχειν ἀναπλάσματα δυναμένοις ἐναργὲς ἦν ψεῦδος. ἆρα γὰρ εὔλογον τὸν τοσαῦτα ὑπὲρ τοῦ γένους τῶν ἀνθρώπων τολμήσαντα, ἵνα τὸ ὅσον ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ πάντες Ἕλληνες καὶ βάρβαροι κρίσιν θείαν προσδοκήσαντες ἀποστῶσι μὲν τῆς κακίας πάντα δὲ πράττωσιν ἀρεσκόντως τῷ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργῷ, παράδοξον μὲν μὴ ἐσχηκέναι γένεσιν πασῶν δὲ γενέσεων παρανομωτάτην καὶ αἰσχίστην; ἐρῶ δὲ ὡς πρὸς Ἕλληνας καὶ μάλιστα Κέλσον, εἴτε φρονοῦντα εἴτε μὴ, πλὴν παρατιθέμενον τὰ Πλάτωνος· ἆρα ὁ καταπέμπων ψυχὰς εἰς ἀνθρώπων σώματα τὸν τοσαῦτα τολμήσοντα καὶ τοσούτους διδάξοντα καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς χύσεως τῆς κατὰ τὴν κακίαν μεταστήσοντα πολλοὺς ἀνθρώπων ἐπὶ τὴν πασῶν αἰσχροτέραν γένεσιν ὤθει, μηδὲ διὰ γάμων γνησίων αὐτὸν εἰσαγαγὼν εἰς τὸν τῶν ἀνθρώπων βίον; ἢ εὐλογώτερον ἑκάστην ψυχὴν κατά τινας ἀποῤῥήτους λόγους (λέγω δὲ ταῦτα νῦν κατὰ Πυθαγόραν καὶ Πλάτωνα καὶ Ἐμπεδοκλέα, οὓς πολλάκις ὠνόμασεν ὁ Κέλσος,) εἰσκρινομένην σώματι κατ᾿ ἀξίαν εἰσκρίνεσθαι καὶ κατὰ τὰ πρότερα ἤθη; εἰκὸς οὖν καὶ ταύτην τὴν ψυχὴν, πολλῶν (ἵνα μὴ συναρπάζειν δοκῶ, λέγων πάντων) ἀνθρώπων ὠφελιμωτέραν τῷ βίῳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπιδημοῦσαν, δεδεῆσθαι σώματος, οὐ μόνον ὡς ἐν ἀνθρωπίνοις σώμασι διαφέροντος ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦ πάντων κρείττονος.
pass_a_gloss: But let us return to the Jew's characterisation (προσωποποιΐα), in which Jesus' mother is written up as thrust out (ἐξωθέω) by the carpenter (τέκτων) who was betrothed (μνηστεύομαι) to her, convicted of adultery (μοιχεία), and bearing [a child] from a certain soldier (στρατιώτης) named Panthera (Πανθήρα); and let us see whether those who mythologised (μυθοποιέω) the adultery of the virgin and Panthera and the carpenter thrusting her out did not blindly (τυφλῶς) fabricate (ἀναπλάσσω) all these for the overthrow (καθαίρεσις) of the paradoxical/miraculous (παράδοξος) conception (σύλληψις) from the Holy Spirit (ἅγιον πνεῦμα). For they could otherwise have lied (ψευδοποιέω) about the story, because of its being very paradoxical, and not as if unwillingly (ἀκουσίως) concede (συγκατατίθεμαι) that Jesus was not born from marriages (γάμοι) customary to men. And it was consistent (ἀκόλουθον) that those not assenting to Jesus' paradoxical birth should fabricate some lie (ψεῦδος); but their not doing this plausibly, but with keeping (τηρέω) that the virgin did not conceive (συλλαμβάνω) Jesus from Joseph, was an evident (ἐναργές) lie to those able to hear and refute fabrications (ἀναπλάσματα). For is it reasonable (εὔλογον) that he who dared so much for the human race, so that, as far as in him, all Greeks and barbarians, expecting divine judgment (κρίσις θεία), might depart from vice and do all things pleasingly (ἀρεσκόντως) to the Craftsman/Creator of the universe (δημιουργὸς τῶν ὅλων), had not a paradoxical birth but the most lawless (παρανομωτάτη) and most shameful (αἰσχίστη) of all births? I will speak as to Greeks and especially Celsus, whether thinking [so] or not, but citing (παρατίθεμαι) Plato's [words]: did he who sends down (καταπέμπω) souls into men's bodies push (ὠθέω) the one about to dare so much, teach so many, and transfer many men from the outpouring/dissipation (χύσις) of vice, into the most shameful birth of all, not even leading him into human life through legitimate marriages (γάμοι γνήσιοι)? Or is it more reasonable that each soul, according to certain secret reasons (I say this now according to Pythagoras, Plato and Empedocles, whom Celsus often named), being introduced (εἰσκρίνομαι) into a body is introduced according to worth (κατ᾿ ἀξίαν) and according to former characters (ἤθη)? It is likely, then, that this soul too, sojourning (ἐπιδημέω) in the life of men more beneficial (ὠφελιμωτέρα) than many men (so that I may not seem to seize [the point] unfairly (συναρπάζω) by saying 'all'), needed a body not only differing as among human bodies but the strongest/best of all (πάντων κρείττων).
pass_b_english: But let us return to the speech Celsus puts in the mouth of his Jew. There the mother of Jesus is described as having been driven out by the carpenter who was betrothed to her, after being convicted of adultery, and as having borne a child by a certain soldier named Panthera. Let us see whether those who made up the tale of the virgin’s adultery with Panthera, and of the carpenter’s driving her out, did not invent all this blindly, in order to overthrow the miraculous conception by the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:18–20; Luke 1:35). For, because the story was so very wonderful, they could have falsified it in some other way, instead of conceding, as if against their will, that Jesus was not born of an ordinary human marriage. It was to be expected that those who did not accept Jesus’ miraculous birth would invent some lie. But they did not do it convincingly: they held on to the fact that the virgin did not conceive Jesus by Joseph. So, to those able to listen and to expose fabrications, the lie was obvious.

For is it reasonable that he who dared so much for the human race, so that, as far as lay in him, all Greeks and barbarians, looking for divine judgment, might turn away from wickedness and do everything in a way pleasing to the Creator of the universe, should have had no miraculous birth, but the most lawless and shameful birth of all?

I will speak as to Greeks, and especially to Celsus, who, whether he holds these views or not, at any rate cites Plato’s words. Would he who sends souls down into human bodies thrust one who was to dare so much, to teach so many, and to turn many people from the flood of wickedness, into the most shameful birth of all, not even bringing him into human life through lawful marriage? Or is it more reasonable that each soul, for certain secret reasons (I say this now following Pythagoras, Plato and Empedocles, whom Celsus has often named), when it is put into a body, is put there according to its desert and its former character? It is likely, then, that this soul too, which came to dwell in human life and was of more benefit to it than many men (I do not say “all,” so as not to seem to be forcing the argument), needed a body that was not only outstanding among human bodies but the best of all.

choices.choice: Celsus's Panthera charge is again reported indirectly ('is described'), not quoted, so no quotation marks. 'The conception by the Holy Spirit' cites Matthew 1:18–20 (ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου) and Luke 1:35; the betrothal and the carpenter echo Matthew 1:18 and 13:55 but are Celsus's framing. 'The flood of wickedness' (χύσις τῆς κακίας, 'outpouring, dissipation') repeats the phrase of 1.26. The soul-descent doctrine is presented as Plato's, Pythagoras's and Empedocles's, without a single passage named, so no classical citation is given (compare in general the myth of Er, Republic 10). συναρπάζειν, 'to snatch [assent]', rendered 'forcing the argument'. κρείττονος rendered 'the best of all'. The argument continues into 1.33.
